sentences.text: This genus is known only from isolated teeth discovered across Europe, Africa, and Asia. It is distinguished by a rectangular tooth root and a twisted blade, a combination unique among mackerel sharks.
The genus was first described by Leidy in 1877.

Later species include Xiphodolamia barbadica described by Casier in 1958, Xiphodolamia maliki by Artüz and Sakınç in 2025, Xiphodolamia morricei by Jordan and Beal in 1910, and Xiphodolamia serrata by Adnet and colleagues in 2009.
It is assumed to have been a pelagic shark living in deeper waters, with fossils found in deposits like the London Clay and Eocene strata in Denmark.

Xiphodolamia serrata is a serrated variety known from the Upper Eocene of Africa and Arabia. The development of serrations in this species mirrors that of Otodus in the Ypresian, representing an example of convergent evolution.
The consensus classification places this animal as an unusual member of the order Lamniformes within the class Chondrichthyes. Some researchers have placed it in its own family, Xiphodolamiidae.
Xiphodolamia lived from the Ypresian to the Messinian, spanning from 56 to 5.333 million years ago.

It is unclear what ecological niche the specialized dentition of Xiphodolamia helped the animal exploit. The exact placement of Xiphodolamia within Lamniformes remains uncertain, particularly regarding its relationship to Lamnidae and Isurus.
